## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="merit-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Supply stack</dt><dd>All offers lined up from cheapest to dearest, each as wide as its MW and as high as its offer.</dd>
<dt>Clearing price</dt><dd>The offer of the marginal plant, the one that serves the last MW of demand; every running plant is paid it.</dd>
<dt>Gas sets the price, often</dt><dd>When a gas plant is marginal, each $1 per MMBtu on gas adds its heat rate in dollars to every MWh that hour.</dd>
<dt>More wind, lower prices</dt><dd>Wind's offer is about $0, so new wind pushes dearer plants out of the stack and lowers the price for everyone.</dd>
<dt>Below zero</dt><dd>The price turns negative only when the last plant needed would pay to keep running: a credit per MWh, or high costs to stop and restart.</dd>
<dt>An optimization in disguise</dt><dd>The stack is the cheapest way to meet demand; the price is the cost of one more MWh, the shadow price of supply equals demand.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<style>/* lesson-local: keep Go deeper text inside the card on phones; wide equations scroll on their own (requested for deeper.css) */
.page-lesson .lx-deeper-body{grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr)}.page-lesson .lx-deeper-body .math.display{overflow-x:auto;overflow-y:hidden}</style>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Economic dispatch as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For one hour, with $p_g$ the output of plant $g$ in MW, $c_g$ its offer in \$/MWh, $\bar P_g$ what it can make this hour and $D$ the demand:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{p}\;\; & \textstyle\sum_g c_g\, p_g \\
\text{subject to}\;\; & \textstyle\sum_g p_g = D \quad (\lambda)\\
& 0 \le p_g \le \bar P_g \quad (\text{each } g).
\end{aligned}
$$

Every term is linear, so this is a [linear program]{.lx-term term="linear-program"}. At 19:00, with $c = (0, 0, 10, 40, 100)$, $\bar P = (72, 14, 100, 150, 100)$ and $D = 331$, the answer is $p = (72, 14, 100, 145, 0)$ and a running cost of $100 \times 10 + 145 \times 40 = \$6{,}800$. With $D = 332$ it is \$6,840: the [shadow price]{.lx-term term="shadow-price"} $\lambda$ of the balance rule is \$40 per MWh, the clearing price.

[Lesson 0](00-grid-operator.html) wrote the same problem over 24 hours with a ramp limit. The ramp limit ties the hours together, which is why the peaker ran there at moments when a single hour's stack would not call it.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Prices from a solver, and where this one-hour picture stops</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>M1 (upcoming in the Modeler tier) builds a 24-hour dispatch linear program with ramps, adds a three-bus network, fills a line and reads one price per bus from the solver.</li>
<li>Lesson 11 (upcoming) hands a linear program to a real solver and reads its prices.</li>
<li>With on/off decisions and start-up costs (M2, upcoming), no single price covers every plant's costs; markets add side payments, called uplift.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this one-hour stack leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Offers are not always costs: sellers can add a mark-up, and market monitors watch for it.</li>
<li>Start-up costs, minimum outputs and ramp limits, which link one hour to the next.</li>
<li>Reserves held back for surprises (lesson 3), and the network, which the last step only hints at.</li>
<li>Many markets clear a day ahead and again in real time, and cap prices in shortages.</li>
<li>Demand that answers the price, such as batteries and flexible users (lesson 9 and A3, upcoming).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m8-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="paid" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Each plant is paid the price it offered.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In a uniform-price market every running plant is paid the clearing price: at 19:00 the solar farm offers $0.00 and is paid $40.00.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The wholesale price is the average cost of the plants that run.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is the offer of the last plant needed, the marginal plant, not an average.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wind" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “More wind can lower the price of every MWh in that hour.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. At 19:00 a 475 MW wind farm pushes the combined-cycle plant out of the stack, and the price falls from $40.00 to $10.00.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="negative" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A negative price means the grid has failed.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It means the last plant needed would pay to keep running; it signals more power in that place than can be used right then.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m8">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="stack" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">Offers: wind 80 MW at $0, a 100 MW plant at $10, a 150 MW plant at $40 and a 100 MW plant at $100. Demand is 250 MW. What is the clearing price?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$0</li><li data-value="b">$10</li><li data-value="c">$40</li><li data-value="d">$100</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$40: the first two offers cover 180 MW, so the $40 plant serves the last 70 MW and sets the price.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gas" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A combined-cycle plant that burns 6 MMBtu per MWh is marginal. Gas rises from $6 to $8 per MMBtu. How much does the price rise?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$2 per MWh</li><li data-value="b">$6 per MWh</li><li data-value="c">$12 per MWh</li><li data-value="d">$48 per MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$12 per MWh: 6 MMBtu × $2 more per MMBtu.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::
